relationship: Dialogue echo: mortal righteousness
rationale: Job asks how a mortal can be righteous before the Lord, taking up the question of mortal purity and blamelessness in Eliphaz's reported speech. The repeated question does not endorse every conclusion Eliphaz draws about Job.

relationship: Prayer and judgment parallel
rationale: Job's question about a mortal being righteous before the Lord parallels the psalm's plea not to enter judgment because no living person will be justified before Him. Both frame the difficulty as standing in divine judgment.

relationship: Narrative development: inability to answer
rationale: Job anticipates being unable to answer even one divine word out of a thousand. When addressed by the Lord, he later asks what answer he can give, covers his mouth and says he will add nothing.

relationship: Recurring image: mountains wearing away
rationale: Job describes God wearing out and overturning mountains; he later compares human endurance with a falling mountain and a rock worn from its place. The repeated landscape imagery concerns vulnerability, without identifying one geological event.

relationship: Cosmic pillars: contrasting actions
rationale: Job describes the world's foundations shaking and its pillars swaying; the psalm describes the earth melting and its pillars being established. Both express control over the world's stability through the particular image of pillars.

relationship: Cosmic judgment imagery
rationale: Job attributes the sun's failure to rise and the sealing of stars to divine command. Isaiah's account of the Lord's day likewise describes stars withholding light and the rising sun darkening; the passages do not identify the same occasion.

relationship: Creation imagery: stretched heaven
rationale: Job says God alone stretched out heaven; Isaiah describes Him stretching it like a dwelling tent. Both attribute heaven's extension to God, with Isaiah supplying the tent comparison.

relationship: Narrative comparison: walking on the sea
rationale: Job describes God walking on the sea as on ground. Matthew depicts Jesus approaching the disciples by walking on the sea and identifying Himself to their frightened group. The comparison concerns this distinctive action, without turning Job's line into a narrated forecast of that voyage.

relationship: Divine speech revisits the constellations
rationale: Job names the Pleiades, Evening Star and Arcturus among God's works. The Lord later asks him about the Pleiades, Orion, mazourōth and the Evening Star. The named heavenly bodies overlap, but the two lists are not made identical.

relationship: Repeated wording across disputants
rationale: Job repeats Eliphaz's description of great, unsearchable, glorious and extraordinary works beyond numbering. Their shared praise of divine power therefore coexists with their disagreement about Job's suffering.

relationship: Recurring complaint: unseen divine action
rationale: Job cannot perceive God passing him; later he says he did not grasp God's action on the left and will not see Him at the right. Both distinguish divine activity from Job's inability to apprehend it.

relationship: Recurring question: unopposable divine action
rationale: Job asks who can turn God back or demand what He has done. He later asks who contradicted God's judgment and says God did whatever He wished, repeating the difficulty of contesting divine action.

relationship: Contrast within Job's legal argument
rationale: Job initially says even his righteousness would not secure a hearing and he must plead for judgment. Later he declares that he is near judgment and knows he will be shown righteous. The comparison preserves the movement in his confidence rather than flattening both statements.

relationship: Recurring complaint: an unheard cry
rationale: Job doubts that God has heard him even if an answer comes; later he explicitly complains that he cried and God does not hear. The later protest sharpens the earlier uncertainty about a hearing.

relationship: Complaint tested against the prologue
rationale: Job describes injuries multiplied without cause. In the prologue the Lord affirms Job's continuing innocence and says the devil urged destruction of his belongings for nothing. The narrative supports the distinction between suffering and a demonstrated offense by Job.

relationship: Shared lament: filled with bitterness
rationale: Job says God has filled him with bitterness; the lamenting speaker likewise says He filled him with bitterness and made him drunk with gall. Both use filling imagery for suffering attributed to divine action.

relationship: Contrast: strength and a hearing
rationale: Job initially asks who can resist God's overwhelming strength in judgment. Later he envisages great strength without threat and asks for his case to reach its conclusion, expressing a changed hope about the same unequal encounter.

relationship: Anticipated and asserted self-condemnation
rationale: Job fears that his own mouth will act impiously even if he is righteous. Eliphaz later says Job's mouth and lips will reprove and testify against him. Job's apprehension and his friend's accusation remain distinct positions.

relationship: Contrast in professions of innocence
rationale: Job says he does not know in his soul whether he acted impiously, knowing only that his life is being taken. Later he refuses to surrender innocence and says he is not conscious of improper deeds. The link preserves these different formulations of self-knowledge.

relationship: Recurring protest: righteous people mocked
rationale: Job says the righteous are mocked, then describes a righteous and blameless man becoming an object of mockery. The latter line makes personal and explicit the injustice he already names here.

relationship: Recurring complaint: handed to the ungodly
rationale: Job describes people handed into an ungodly person's hands and later says the Lord handed him into an unjust person's hands. The shared handover language belongs to Job's protest, not a new identification of the unnamed oppressor.

relationship: Recurring image: life passing swiftly
rationale: Job calls his life swifter than a runner after describing it as lighter than chatter and perishing in empty hope. Both images present his life as rapidly escaping him, while retaining the source's different comparisons.

relationship: Shared paired images: eagle and ship paths
rationale: Job asks about the trace of a ship's way and an eagle seeking food. Proverbs likewise pairs the tracks of a flying eagle with a seagoing ship's paths among things difficult to comprehend. The matching pair is more specific than a general statement about life's brevity.

relationship: Shared paired images: vanished passage
rationale: Job's question about a ship's trace and an eagle's flight parallels the ship and bird whose passage leaves no trace in Wisdom. Wisdom places those images in the speech of the repentant wrongdoers; that speaker identity is not assigned to Job.

relationship: Recurring anxiety about acquittal
rationale: Job fears God will not leave him innocent. He next says lawlessness has not been acquitted and that even righteousness leaves him unable to look up, extending the same concern about his standing before God.

relationship: Cleansing imagery with different claims
rationale: Job imagines washing with snow and clean hands, yet in the following line remains in filth. Jeremiah says washing with natron and cleansing herb leaves injustice stained before God. The shared failure of washing does not establish that Job bears the particular apostasy accused in Jeremiah.

relationship: Contrast: filthy garments and their removal
rationale: Job says he has been plunged into filth and his own robe abhors him. Joshua's filthy garments are instead removed and replaced as his lawless deeds are taken away. The garment comparison contrasts Job's complaint with a narrated act of cleansing.

relationship: Divine and human distinction
rationale: Job cannot litigate with God as with a fellow human being. Balaam's utterance likewise says God is not as a man, there emphasizing that He is not led astray or threatened and fulfills His words. The shared distinction serves different arguments.

relationship: Mediation: request and explicit identification
rationale: Job wishes for a mediator who can hear the cause between both sides. First Timothy explicitly names Christ Jesus as the mediator between God and humanity and speaks of His ransom. This compares the mediating role; Job's unnamed desired mediator is not treated as an explicit personal identification.

relationship: Repeated conditions for speaking
rationale: Job asks for the rod and terror to be removed so he can speak. His later two requests again seek the withdrawal of God's hand and overwhelming terror before an exchange of speech.

relationship: Repeated declaration of bitter speech
rationale: Job announces that he will let his words loose and speak from bitterness, repeating his earlier refusal to restrain his mouth while disclosing his soul's bitterness. Both mark his deliberate decision to voice the complaint.

relationship: Legal protest and request for disclosure
rationale: Job asks why the Lord judged him this way, alongside his plea not to be taught to act impiously. Later he asks to be taught how many sins and lawless deeds he has. Both seek an explanation of the charge, without replacing this verse's unusual wording.

relationship: Appeal concerning the maker's handiwork
rationale: Job protests that he might disown the works of God's hands while God attends to ungodly counsel. The psalm pleads that the Lord not neglect the works of His hands. The link concerns the appeal to created handiwork, preserving the different subjects of disowning and neglecting.

relationship: Divine sight distinguished from human sight
rationale: Job asks whether God sees as a mortal. In Samuel's encounter with Jesse's sons, God explicitly distinguishes human attention to the face from His own attention to the heart. Both contrast the modes of divine and human seeing.

relationship: Divine duration and human time
rationale: Job asks whether God's years are those of a man. Moses' prayer contrasts God's existence from age to age with a thousand years like yesterday or a watch in the night, supplying a particular comparison of divine and human time.

relationship: Contrast in requests for divine examination
rationale: Job questions why God investigates his sins. The psalm instead asks God to examine the heart and paths and discover any way of lawlessness. Both concern divine scrutiny of wrongdoing, approached as complaint and invitation respectively.

relationship: Claim of innocence and narrative testimony
rationale: Job appeals to God's knowledge that he did not act impiously. The prologue has the Lord affirm his innocence and blamelessness even after loss, providing narrative context for his claim without endorsing every later accusation he makes.

relationship: Shared formula: no rescue from God's hands
rationale: Job asks who can rescue from God's hands. The divine declaration in Moses' song similarly says no one can deliver from His hands, alongside His power to kill, make alive, strike and heal.

relationship: Creator's hands invoked amid affliction
rationale: Job sets God's molding hands against the subsequent blow. Isaiah's communal prayer calls the people clay and the work of God's hands, then asks Him not to be exceedingly angry. Both appeal to the maker-creature relation during distress.

relationship: Formation from earth
rationale: Job recalls being molded as clay; Genesis narrates God forming the human from the earth's dust. The correspondence is the divine shaping of an earthly body, not a claim that the two accounts use identical material terms.

relationship: Return to the material of formation
rationale: Job says God is turning him back into earth. The sentence to Adam likewise speaks of returning to the earth from which he was taken, connecting mortal dissolution with earthly formation.

relationship: The body as divine handiwork
rationale: Job describes being clothed with skin and flesh and threaded with bones and sinews. The psalm speaks of God's knowledge and making of the body's hidden bone and unworked substance in the context of the womb. These are particular depictions of embodied formation, not identical anatomical accounts.

relationship: Repeated confession of divine possibility
rationale: Job's acknowledgment that God can do all things and nothing is impossible for Him recurs in his final reply to the Lord. The repeated wording spans the complaint and the concluding response.

relationship: Recurring plea concerning unremoved sin
rationale: Job says lawlessness has not been acquitted after previously asking why forgetfulness and cleansing of his sin had not been granted. Both make the absence of release from sin part of his address to God.

relationship: Righteousness without security
rationale: Job says neither being ungodly nor being righteous permits him to lift his face. Earlier he feared that even righteousness and blamelessness would end with an impious mouth and a crooked result. Both express his sense that innocence does not secure a fair outcome.

relationship: Lament imagery: hunted by a lion
rationale: Job describes being hunted like a lion for slaughter. Lamentations portrays the divine adversary as a hidden lion who pursues and desolates the speaker. Both employ predation imagery for affliction, but Job is the hunted comparison while the lament describes the pursuer.

relationship: Recurring forensic complaint
rationale: Job complains that examination against him is renewed in anger; later he says evils have been recorded against him and the sins of youth put around him. Both express the sense of an accumulating divine case against him.

relationship: Repeated wish concerning birth and death
rationale: Job asks why he was brought from the womb rather than dying unseen. His opening lament already asked why he did not die in the womb or perish immediately upon coming out.

relationship: Repeated image: existence without seeing life
rationale: Job wishes he had passed from womb to tomb as though he never existed. The earlier comparison with a miscarriage or infants who never saw light expresses the same counterfactual wish without identifying it as an actual event.

relationship: Repeated request for brief respite
rationale: Job asks to rest a little because his lifetime is short. Earlier he asked to be left alone because he would not live forever and wanted even enough respite to swallow, giving concrete form to the same appeal.

relationship: Recurring description of departure without return
rationale: Job anticipates going to a land from which he will not return. Earlier he described descent to Hades as not returning to one's house or recognized place. These remain statements within his lament.

relationship: Many words and the claim to righteousness
rationale: Zophar challenges the righteousness of an eloquent, much-speaking person. Proverbs warns that much talking does not escape sin and commends sparing the lips. The proverb parallels the warning about speech, without proving Zophar's accusation against Job.

relationship: Disputed profession of innocence
rationale: Zophar tells Job not to claim purity and blamelessness before God. Job had just appealed to God's knowledge that he did not act impiously. The link identifies a specific claim under dispute between the speakers.

relationship: Requested divine speech and eventual answer
rationale: Zophar wishes the Lord would speak to Job. The narrative later records the Lord speaking through a whirlwind and requiring Job to answer. That eventual speech does not itself validate Zophar's following accusation about deserved suffering.

relationship: Narrative correction of a friend's verdict
rationale: Zophar says Job's suffering is worthy of his committed sins. The closing narrative instead includes Zophar among the friends who did not speak truth against Job and who require his offering and prayer. The narrative verdict prevents treating Zophar's sentence as an established explanation of Job's affliction.

relationship: Unsearchable divine wisdom
rationale: Zophar asks whether Job can find the Lord's trace or reach the furthest divine works. Paul's doxology describes divine judgments as unsearchable and ways as untraceable, then asks who knew His mind or became His counselor. The wisdom comparison does not adopt Zophar's personal charges.

relationship: Heaven and Hades as limits of human reach
rationale: Zophar uses heaven's height and depths beyond Hades to challenge human knowledge. The psalm pairs ascent to heaven and descent into Hades to describe God's presence. The shared vertical extremes serve distinct arguments about knowledge and presence.

relationship: A question repeated by an opponent
rationale: Zophar's question, who can say to God what He has done, repeats Job's own question. Their agreement about unopposable divine action does not settle their disagreement about Job's guilt.

relationship: Divine knowledge of lawless conduct
rationale: Zophar says God knows lawless works and will not overlook improper things. Elihu later states that no human action escapes God and lawless people have nowhere to hide. The two speakers share this assertion without its proving their specific charges against Job.

relationship: Prayer joined to inward turning
rationale: Zophar urges purity of heart and hands turned upward toward God. Lamentations joins a return to the Lord with lifting hearts upon hands to the Exalted One in heaven. Both combine inward turning and an embodied prayer gesture.

relationship: Removing wrongdoing before supplication
rationale: Zophar requires lawlessness to be removed from the hands and dwelling. Isaiah's rebuke of blood-filled praying hands likewise calls for washing, removing evil deeds and seeking justice. This is a comparison of the prescribed response, not evidence that Job committed the crimes Isaiah condemns.

relationship: Conflicting cleansing expectations
rationale: Zophar promises a face like pure water and removal of filth. Job had imagined washing himself yet being plunged into filth. Their opposing outcomes for cleansing express a concrete disagreement about Job's prospects before God.

relationship: Promised forgetting of former affliction
rationale: Zophar promises Job that toil will be forgotten like a passing wave. Isaiah likewise promises that former affliction will be forgotten and not enter the heart, within a wider account of renewal. The common promise does not identify Zophar's assurance with Isaiah's setting.

relationship: Light at noon as an image of restoration
rationale: Zophar compares prayer to the morning star and says life will rise from noon. The psalm promises righteousness like light and judgment like noon. The link preserves Zophar's particular prayer-and-life wording while comparing the use of bright-day imagery for vindication or renewal.

relationship: Narrative reversal: others entreating Job
rationale: Zophar predicts that many will change their ways and entreat Job. At the end, Zophar himself joins the other friends in going to Job as commanded for the offering and prayer through which their sin is released. This is a particular reversal of the adviser's role.

relationship: Shared warning: the ungodly person's hope
rationale: Zophar concludes that the ungodly person's hope is destruction; Bildad had likewise said that the hope of an ungodly person will perish. These parallel conclusions belong to the friends' speeches and do not independently establish Job's guilt.

relationship: Rebuke of exclusive wisdom
rationale: Job sarcastically says wisdom must die with his companions, then explicitly says he knows as much as they do and is not less intelligent. The second assertion makes the force of the earlier sarcasm clear.

relationship: Repeated claim of equal understanding
rationale: Job's claim to have a heart like his companions is developed as knowing as much as they know and being no less intelligent. The two statements reject their assumed intellectual superiority.

relationship: Narrative characterization and humiliating treatment
rationale: Job describes a righteous and blameless man made a mockery. Those are characteristics the narrator gives Job at the book's opening, making the mismatch between his characterization and treatment particularly significant.

relationship: Agreement that wickedness faces examination
rationale: Job warns wicked people not to suppose they will escape examination. Elihu later likewise rejects the claim that a man faces no inspection from the Lord. This comparison retains the actual warning in 12:6 instead of importing a different wording about secure robbers' tents.

relationship: Learning through nonhuman creatures
rationale: Job directs his listeners to ask animals and birds for instruction. Proverbs tells the sluggard to observe the ant and learn from the bee. Both use nonhuman creatures as teachers, with different lessons and named creatures.

relationship: Creation of the creatures invoked as witnesses
rationale: Job says these creatures know the Lord's hand made them, after naming land animals, birds and fish. Genesis narrates God's making of sea creatures, winged birds and land animals, providing the corresponding creation account for those classes.

relationship: Every life and breath dependent on God
rationale: Job places all living things and every human breath in God's hand. Paul's speech similarly describes the creator as giving everyone life and breath and sustaining human existence. Both specify universal bodily dependence on the creator.

relationship: Repeated analogy: ear and throat
rationale: Elihu later repeats Job's comparison of an ear testing words with a throat tasting food. The same sensory analogy is used by different speakers in their effort to evaluate the debate.

relationship: Age and wisdom reconsidered
rationale: Job associates wisdom and knowledge with long life. Elihu recalls having deferred to age for that reason but then attributes instruction to the Almighty's breath and denies that elders necessarily know judgment. The comparison preserves Elihu's qualification of the assumption.

relationship: Divine possession and giving of wisdom
rationale: Job locates wisdom, power, counsel and understanding with God. Daniel blesses the Lord for wisdom and majesty and for giving wisdom and understanding, moving from divine possession to its gift to humans.

relationship: Narrative illustration: destructive released water
rationale: Job describes water let loose to destroy the earth. The flood narrative depicts rising waters covering mountains and destroying life on dry land. It illustrates the kind of power Job names without claiming that his general statement explicitly identifies Noah's flood.

relationship: Narrative illustration: restrained water
rationale: Job contrasts released destructive waters with restraint that dries the earth. Genesis describes God bringing a wind, closing the fountains and floodgates, restraining rain and causing waters to withdraw. The link concerns the particular reversal of flooding through divine restraint.

relationship: Counselors and rulers deprived of sound judgment
rationale: Job describes counselors led captive and judges confused. Isaiah's Egypt oracle depicts royal counselors becoming foolish and rulers leading the country astray. This compares the collapse of governing wisdom, not a direct prediction of that oracle's events.

relationship: Divine appointment of kings
rationale: Job says God seats kings on thrones; Daniel says He transfers kings and appoints them. The link retains the actual enthroning wording in Job, rather than replacing it with an alternative about loosening kings' bonds.

relationship: Historical illustration: priests carried captive
rationale: Job says God sends priests captive and overturns rulers. The fall of Judah includes the capture and removal of the first priest and other officials to the Babylonian king. The episode illustrates captured religious and civil leaders without becoming an identified prediction in Job.

relationship: Shared reversal: rulers dishonored, poor helped
rationale: Job pairs dishonor poured on rulers with healing of the lowly. The psalm similarly pairs contempt poured on rulers with help for the poor. The two-part reversal is more specific than a general statement about divine power.

relationship: Shared image: deep darkness disclosed
rationale: Job says God uncovers deep things from darkness and brings death's shadow to light. Daniel praises Him for revealing deep and dark things and knowing darkness and light. Both express hidden knowledge being accessible to God through the same clustered imagery.

relationship: Divine governance of nations' movement and downfall
rationale: Job attributes nations' leading, lowering and destruction to God. Amos places several peoples' movements under His action and then announces the removal of a sinful kingdom. The comparison concerns nations as objects of divine governance without equating the unnamed peoples in Job with one specific kingdom.

relationship: Shared image: rulers wandering off a road
rationale: Job describes earthly rulers' changed hearts and wandering on a road they did not know. The psalm describes rulers wandering in an impassable place that is not a road. Both join rulers' humiliation with loss of a navigable route.

relationship: Shared image: leaders wandering like drunkards
rationale: Job concludes his account of rulers with wandering like a drunk person. Isaiah describes Egypt's leaders being led astray like one wandering drunk and vomiting. The distinctive drunken-wandering comparison accompanies failed leadership in both.

relationship: Hearing and seeing reconsidered
rationale: Job appeals to what his eye has seen and ear heard as credentials in the dispute. His final response contrasts earlier hearing with now seeing God. The later claim is a new encounter, not an assertion that the earlier sight was already that encounter.

relationship: Repeated claim to understanding equal to the friends
rationale: Job says he knows as much as his companions and is not less intelligent, spelling out his earlier assertion that he too has a heart like theirs. Both resist the friends' claim to superior discernment.

relationship: Recurring desire to state a case before God
rationale: Job wants to speak and argue before the Lord if He is willing. Later he wishes to find Him, state his case, fill his mouth with arguments and hear the response, expanding the same legal request.

relationship: Failed care: physicians and comforters
rationale: Job calls the friends unjust physicians and healers of evils, and later comforters of evils. The repeated description criticizes their failure in the caring role for which they came.

relationship: Silence reckoned as wisdom
rationale: Job says silence would become wisdom for his companions. Proverbs similarly says someone who makes himself mute will seem intelligent. Both invert the assumption that speaking demonstrates understanding.

relationship: Narrative response to allegedly false speech before God
rationale: Job accuses the friends of speaking deceit before the Lord. At the conclusion the Lord tells Eliphaz and his companions that they spoke nothing true before Him and did not speak truth against Job. The later verdict addresses the very issue Job raises.

relationship: Anticipated divine reproof of the friends
rationale: Job warns that God will reprove the friends despite their position in the debate. The final narrative records that reproof and requires them to seek the offering and prayer of the man they accused.

relationship: Condemnation of partiality
rationale: Job warns that secretly admiring persons will not escape divine reproof. James likewise calls favoritism sin and says the law convicts its practitioners. The comparison concerns partiality, not an identity between the two audiences.

relationship: Divine terror turned toward the advisers
rationale: Job asks whether divine terror will overwhelm his friends, after asking that such terror be removed from himself. The repeated terror language turns their discussion toward their own exposure to divine judgment.

relationship: Clay mortality turned back on the adviser
rationale: Job says the friends' bodies will be clay. Eliphaz's earlier reported message described humans dwelling in houses of clay and perishing within a day. Job applies the bodily fragility they invoked to the advisers themselves.

relationship: Speech sought as relief
rationale: Job asks for silence so he may speak and rest from anger. Elihu later says he will speak so he may rest, opening his lips. The repeated purpose of obtaining relief through speech belongs to different speakers.

relationship: Shared idiom: life placed in one's hand
rationale: Job speaks of putting his life in his hand as he insists on speaking. Jonathan describes David placing his soul in his hand when striking the foreigner. The comparison is the idiom of personal exposure to danger, not an identification of the actions.

relationship: Persistence in pleading despite divine pressure
rationale: Job says he will speak and plead even as the Mighty One subdues him. Later he describes presenting arguments and asking the powerful God to conclude his case. This preserves the source's resolve to plead; it does not import an alternative wording about trusting if slain.

relationship: Deceit excluded from the divine presence
rationale: Job expects deliverance because deceit will not enter before God. The psalm says evildoers cannot sojourn with Him or remain before His eyes and that He destroys speakers of falsehood. Both connect access to the divine presence with exclusion of deceit.

relationship: Expected vindication and the Lord's stated purpose
rationale: Job says he knows he will be shown righteous. The Lord later asks whether His dealing with Job had any purpose other than that Job might be shown righteous. The close verbal link does not make all of Job's preceding judgments correct.

relationship: Forensic challenge to an accuser
rationale: Job asks who will enter judgment with him. Isaiah's speaker, with the justifier near, likewise challenges whoever brings a case to approach. These are comparable legal challenges by distinct speakers.

relationship: Repeated request: remove terror before speech
rationale: Job asks that God's hand and overwhelming terror be kept away. Earlier he asked for removal of the rod and terror so he could speak without fear. Both state conditions he desires for a hearing.

relationship: Requested exchange and eventual demand to answer
rationale: Job proposes that God call or speak and he answer. The Lord later explicitly says He will question Job and Job must answer Him. The eventual encounter places the initiative with God, as this source's wording already does.

relationship: Repeated request to be taught his error
rationale: Job asks to be taught his sins and lawless deeds. Earlier he told the friends to teach him, promising silence if they could tell him where he had gone astray. Both demand a stated offense rather than an unsupported accusation.

relationship: Recurring complaint: treated as an opponent
rationale: Job asks why God regards him as opposed to Him. Later he says God dealt with him in anger and regarded him like an enemy. The latter restates the perceived hostile relationship in the complaint.

relationship: Sins of youth remembered or released
rationale: Job complains that the sins of youth have been put around him. The psalm asks the Lord not to remember youthful sins and acts of ignorance, but to remember the speaker according to mercy. Both explicitly concern the continuing reckoning of youthful wrongdoing.

relationship: Elihu's reprise of Job's complaint
rationale: Job describes a foot in restraint and all his works watched. Elihu later quotes a complaint that God regards the speaker as an opponent, put his foot in a wooden restraint and guarded his ways. The shared restraint and surveillance mark a specific reprise within the debate.

relationship: Shared image: garment consumed by a moth
rationale: Job ends the complaint with growing old like a wineskin or a moth-eaten garment. Isaiah's speaker likewise describes opponents growing old like a garment and being devoured like a moth. The decay imagery is shared, while its application differs.

relationship: Human life from birth burdened by trouble
rationale: Job describes the mortal born of woman as short-lived and full of wrath. Sirach describes the heavy yoke from the mother's womb to the mother of all and lists anger, trouble and fear across social ranks. Both present trouble as a condition of embodied mortal life.

relationship: Shared image: human life as a disappearing flower
rationale: Job compares a mortal to a flower that blossoms and falls away. The psalm likewise compares human days to a field flower that vanishes after wind passes. Both locate human transience in the flower's brief flourishing.

relationship: Repeated question of mortal cleansing
rationale: Job asks who can be clean from filth and answers no one. Bildad later asks how a mortal can be righteous before the Lord and how one born of woman can cleanse himself. The question is shared across opponents, not a settled verdict on Job's particular conduct.

relationship: The numbered limit of mortal life
rationale: Job says a person's months are numbered with God and a fixed time cannot be exceeded. The psalm asks to know the limit and number of one's days, calling them handbreadths. Both make life's bounded duration the subject of prayer.

relationship: Recurring image: life as hired labor
rationale: Job asks to be left quiet to enjoy life like a hired worker. Earlier he likened human existence to a day worker and a hired worker waiting for wages. The comparison develops his request for relief through the same laboring figure.

relationship: Hope expressed through renewed tree growth
rationale: Job contrasts human frailty with a cut tree's hope of blossoming again. Ezekiel's tree oracle speaks of the Lord making a dry tree flourish. Both depict renewal through renewed tree growth, but Ezekiel's royal image is not identified with Job's illustrative tree.

relationship: Water and plant survival in opposing speeches
rationale: Job describes water bringing renewed growth from an aged or dead-looking tree. Bildad had asked whether papyrus or rushes flourish without water and described unwatered plants withering. Their plant images agree about dependence on water but place it within different arguments about hope.

relationship: same-chapter tension: death and renewed life
rationale: Job says the dead mortal is gone and no more, then says that if a person dies he will live and that he waits to come to be again. The comparison preserves both statements and their tension, without rewriting either as a question or supplying a harmonized chronology.

relationship: Shared image: waters and rivers drying away
rationale: Job uses a diminishing sea and dried river in his meditation on mortality. Isaiah's Egypt oracle describes a failing river, dry channels and withering river plants. The same loss of water serves different subjects rather than identifying one event.

relationship: Lament and closing notice about rising again
rationale: Job says the lying-down person will not rise until heaven is no longer stitched together or wake from sleep. The book's closing notice explicitly says Job will rise with those the Lord raises. Both are retained in their narrative positions without erasing the lament's temporal wording.

relationship: Hidden until wrath passes, beside hope for the dead
rationale: Job wishes to be hidden in Hades until divine wrath ceases and then remembered. Isaiah places the dead rising beside an instruction to hide in inner rooms until the Lord's wrath passes. The parallel concerns protected waiting during wrath, while Hades and the inner rooms remain different locations.

relationship: Expectation of renewed life and closing notice
rationale: Job says that a person who dies will live and that he will wait until he comes to be again. The closing notice explicitly states that he will rise with those the Lord raises. The link depends on the affirmative wording actually supplied here.

relationship: Repeated call-and-answer hope
rationale: Job anticipates God calling and his own answer, repeating the proposed divine call and human reply of his earlier request for a hearing. Here the appeal also invokes the works of God's hands.

relationship: Divine counting of human conduct
rationale: Job says God numbered his practices and no sin will pass unnoticed. Later he asks whether God will see his way and count all his steps. Both present divine scrutiny through the particular image of counting one's conduct or steps.

relationship: Stored wrongdoing pictured as a bundle
rationale: Job describes his lawless deeds sealed in a bag. Hosea's utterance speaks of a bundle of injustice and Ephraim's hidden sin. The comparison is the packaging of wrongdoing for reckoning; it does not add a sealed bag to Hosea's wording.

relationship: Recurring image: mountains worn and overturned
rationale: Job's falling mountain and rock worn from its place return to his earlier description of God wearing mountains out and overturning them. The repeated imagery frames human endurance against even apparently durable terrain's vulnerability.

relationship: Loss of knowledge of life among the living
rationale: Job describes a departed man not knowing whether his sons become many or few. Ecclesiastes says the dead know nothing and have no further share in what is done under the sun. Both address loss of awareness or participation in earthly affairs.

relationship: A charge about words answered in kind
rationale: Eliphaz condemns speeches without benefit; Job's next reply challenges the order in words of wind and asks what troubles the friend into answering. The exchange shows the accusation of unhelpful speech returned to the accuser.

relationship: Disputed persistence in speaking before God
rationale: Eliphaz treats Job's words before the Lord as rejection of fear. Job had declared that he would continue speaking and pleading under divine pressure. The link preserves the contrast between Job's explanation of his persistence and Eliphaz's judgment of it.

relationship: Job's feared self-condemnation used by Eliphaz
rationale: Eliphaz says Job's own mouth and lips will reprove and testify against him. Earlier Job feared that his mouth would act impiously even if he was righteous. Eliphaz turns the danger Job named into an accusation.

relationship: Birth before the hills: challenge and Wisdom's claim
rationale: Eliphaz asks whether Job was formed before the hills. Wisdom's speech places her birth before the mountains and hills. The shared pre-mountain language contrasts the wisdom Job is challenged to possess with Wisdom's narrated priority, without identifying Job with Wisdom.

relationship: A claim of equal knowledge returned
rationale: Eliphaz asks what Job knows that the friends do not. Job had just said he knew as much as they and was no less intelligent. The matching challenge reveals a reciprocal dispute over intellectual standing.

relationship: Age offered as authority and later qualified
rationale: Eliphaz appeals to elders older than Job's father. Elihu explains that he initially deferred because the others were older, then denies that longevity guarantees wisdom or judgment. The comparison concerns the disputed authority of age.

relationship: Friends' claims about deserved punishment
rationale: Eliphaz says Job was scourged for few of his sins, whereas Zophar said what came from the Lord was worthy of Job's committed sins. Both presume actual offenses behind suffering, while their statements about its measure differ.

relationship: Reversal of an accusation about speech before God
rationale: Eliphaz accuses Job of bursting out in anger and bringing improper words before the Lord. At the end the Lord rebukes Eliphaz and his two companions for speaking nothing true before Him, as Job did. The narrative turns the issue of culpable speech back upon the accuser.

relationship: Eliphaz repeats his question about mortal righteousness
rationale: Eliphaz asks how a mortal can be blameless or one born of woman righteous. His earlier reported speech asked whether a mortal can be pure before the Lord or blameless through works. Both are his arguments from human limitation.

relationship: Repeated distrust of exalted beings
rationale: Eliphaz says God puts no trust in holy ones and that heaven is not pure before Him. His earlier reported message said God places no trust in servants and finds crookedness in angels. The recurring argument retains the different designations and does not specify the identity of every being concerned.

relationship: Drinking as an image for improper conduct
rationale: Eliphaz describes an unclean man drinking injustice like a drink. Elihu later describes Job as drinking mockery like water. The comparison concerns the distinctive drinking metaphor, while injustice and mockery and the speakers' applications remain distinct.

relationship: Wisdom warranted by the ancestors
rationale: Eliphaz appeals to what wise people report from their fathers. Bildad likewise directed Job to the former generation and the fathers for teaching. Both present ancestral testimony as authority within the dispute.

relationship: Assumed peace followed by downfall
rationale: Eliphaz says overthrow comes when an ungodly person thinks he is at peace. Jeremiah condemns assurances of peace where there is none and announces a fall at visitation. Both contrast confidence in peace with approaching judgment, without equating the accused parties.

relationship: Friends' shared darkness imagery for the wicked
rationale: Eliphaz says the ungodly person must not expect to return from darkness. Bildad later describes removal from light into darkness and calls such places the houses of the unjust. These are parallel portrayals in the friends' speeches, not an independent identification of Job as ungodly.

relationship: Judgment image: the dead as food for birds
rationale: Eliphaz assigns the ungodly person as food for vultures. The covenant curse says the dead will be food for heaven's birds and earthly beasts. The particular image is shared without limiting the wider bird category to vultures or claiming Job is under that covenant curse.

relationship: Stiff-necked opposition to God
rationale: Eliphaz describes the ungodly person stiffening his neck against the Lord. Moses similarly speaks of Israel's stiff neck and provocation of God. Both make bodily stiffness an image of resistance, applied to different subjects.

relationship: Bodily fatness accompanying rebellion
rationale: Eliphaz's hostile figure covers his face with fat and forms a collar on his thighs in the context of resisting God. Moses' song describes Jacob growing fat, thick and broad and forsaking his maker. Both associate luxuriant bodily fatness with rebellion in their respective portrayals.

relationship: Lawless wealth failing to endure
rationale: Eliphaz says the ungodly person's belongings will not remain. Proverbs likewise says property eagerly pursued with lawlessness becomes less, contrasting it with pious increase. The link concerns the failure of unjustly pursued wealth, not proof that Job's former wealth was unjust.

relationship: Shoot and flower withering
rationale: Eliphaz describes the ungodly person's shoot withered by wind and flower falling. Isaiah compares all human flesh and glory to grass and a falling flower. Both use botanical decline for transience, but Isaiah's broader human scope is not restricted to Eliphaz's ungodly figure.

relationship: Plant ruined before its expected completion
rationale: Eliphaz says the cutting is destroyed before its time and its shoot will not grow dense. Bildad described an unharvested plant withering before it drinks. Both use premature plant failure in their account of an ungodly person's end.

relationship: Premature loss of unripe grapes
rationale: Eliphaz compares the ungodly person's fate to unripe grapes harvested too soon. Isaiah describes clusters and vine branches removed before harvest while fruit is unripe. The shared pre-harvest destruction is specific, while Eliphaz's additional olive-blossom image is not attributed to Isaiah.

relationship: Corrupt judgment followed by burning imagery
rationale: Eliphaz says fire will burn the houses of bribe-takers. Isaiah condemns those who justify the ungodly for gifts and then uses the image of a stalk consumed by fire for their ruin. Both connect corrupt reward with fiery judgment, without making Isaiah's stalk into a literal house.

relationship: Shared pregnancy image for wrongdoing
rationale: Eliphaz describes conceiving pains and a belly bearing deceit. The psalm describes labor with injustice, conception of trouble and birth of lawlessness. Both organize wrongdoing through the linked stages of conception and birth.

relationship: Failed fulfillment of the friends' purpose
rationale: Job calls the companions comforters of evils. The narrative introduced their visit as an effort to comfort him and showed their initial silent presence. His criticism measures their later speeches against that stated purpose.

relationship: The accusation of windy speech returned
rationale: Job challenges words of wind, while Bildad had described Job's breath as full of words. The shared speech-and-breath imagery shows Job turning a friend's charge back toward the advisers.

relationship: Shared mocking gesture: shaking the head
rationale: Job imagines speaking against his friends and shaking his head if their lives exchanged places. The psalm describes onlookers sneering, speaking with their lips and shaking their heads. The gesture is the comparison; Job's imagined reversal is not a report that it occurred.

relationship: Affliction represented as testimony against Job
rationale: Job describes being seized and the resulting testimony and answer against his face. His earlier complaint described renewed examination against him. Both treat affliction through forensic language, without replacing this verse's reference to his falsehood with a different reading.

relationship: Recurring image: divine arrows in Job
rationale: Job describes anger and arrows falling upon him, returning to his earlier statement that the Lord's arrows are in his body and stab him when he speaks. Both portray suffering as an armed divine assault from Job's perspective.

relationship: Complaint and prologue: being handed over
rationale: Job says the Lord handed him to an unjust person's hands. In the prologue the Lord hands him to the devil with a limit on his life, after which the devil strikes him. The handover is a narrative comparison; the unnamed unjust person in Job's speech is not thereby identified as the devil.

relationship: Shared image: sufferer made a target
rationale: Job says God set him up like a target. Lamentations likewise says He drew His bow and fixed the speaker as a missile's target. Both make the sufferer the deliberately positioned object of an attack.

relationship: Shared image: missiles striking the kidneys
rationale: Job describes surrounding spears striking his kidneys and gall poured out. Lamentations says arrows from the divine quiver entered the speaker's kidneys. Both use the particular internal wound, retaining the different weapons and additional details.

relationship: Weeping and bodily distress
rationale: Job describes a belly burned from weeping and shadow on his eyelids. The psalm joins copious tears with an eye troubled by anger. Both connect grief with bodily and ocular distress, without changing Job's belly to a face or equating the causes of the eye symptoms.

relationship: Profession of integrity and the narrator's description
rationale: Job says his hands contain nothing unjust and his prayer is pure. The opening narrative calls him true, blameless, righteous and God-fearing, providing the stated narrative characterization against which his profession is heard.

relationship: Integrity and acceptable prayer
rationale: Job joins absence of injustice in his hands with purity of prayer. Proverbs contrasts the impious person's sacrifice with acceptable prayers of those going straight. Both relate conduct and prayer, while the proverb is not an independent ruling on every claim in Job's speech.

relationship: Blood, earth and an unsilenced cry
rationale: Job asks earth not to cover his blood or give his cry a resting place. In Genesis, Abel's blood cries to God from the earth that received it. The distinctive combination of earth, blood and audible appeal supports the comparison without identifying Job with Abel.

relationship: Prayer accompanied by tears
rationale: Job asks that his supplication reach the Lord while his eye pours tears. The psalm similarly asks the Lord to hear supplication and not remain silent at tears. Both explicitly seek a hearing for tearful prayer.

relationship: Recurring request for a hearing between human and God
rationale: Job wishes for a hearing before the Lord and for a son of man to plead for a neighbor. Earlier he wished for a mediator to hear the cause between both sides. The link compares the desired intercession without naming the unspecified advocate.

relationship: Recurring image: a journey without return
rationale: Job says his numbered years bring him to a way on which he will not return. His earlier account of going down to Hades likewise excludes return to one's house and former place. Both belong to his anticipation of death.

relationship: Longed-for death and unavailable burial
rationale: Job says he is perishing and needs burial but cannot obtain it. His first lament described people longing for death without obtaining it and rejoicing if they do. Both portray desired release as unavailable, while death and burial are not treated as identical requests.

relationship: Complaint recalls stolen possessions
rationale: Job says strangers stole his belongings. The opening reports describe raiders carrying off oxen and donkeys and horsemen carrying off camels. These losses give narrative context to the complaint without assigning an ethnicity to the unnamed strangers.

relationship: Understanding withheld from the heart
rationale: Job says God hid their heart from understanding. Moses tells Israel that the Lord had not given a heart to know, eyes to see or ears to hear. Both attribute the absence of understanding to divine withholding, with distinct groups and circumstances.

relationship: Sorrow over sons and the reported loss
rationale: Job speaks of his eyes wasting away over sons. The prologue reports the house collapsing on his sons and daughters and their death, giving concrete narrative context for his sorrow without importing a different rendering about children's eyes failing.

relationship: Recurring humiliation: made a tale
rationale: Job says he became a tale among nations and their laughingstock. Later he says his mockers made him their lyre and repeated tale. Both describe the social circulation of his humiliation.

relationship: Eyes affected by anger amid affliction
rationale: Job describes his eyes hardened by anger and himself besieged. The psalm likewise describes the eye troubled by anger amid affliction, pain and groaning. The comparison preserves the different descriptions of the eyes rather than substituting a familiar rendering about dimness.

relationship: Perseverance in a righteous way
rationale: Job urges a faithful person to hold his way and the clean-handed to take courage. Later he declares that he will not abandon innocence or let go of righteousness. The personal declaration develops the perseverance urged here.

relationship: Repeated rejection of the friends' counsel
rationale: Job finds nothing true among those he addresses. Earlier he called all the friends unjust physicians and healers of evils. Both reject the collective adequacy of their counsel, rather than identifying a new group of visitors.

relationship: Hades replacing the earthly house
rationale: Job anticipates Hades as his house and gloom as his bedding. Earlier he said the person descending to Hades would not return to his own house. The lodging imagery makes his expected displacement from home concrete.

relationship: Question about future good and narrative restoration
rationale: Job asks where hope remains and whether he will see good things. The conclusion records restored relationships, consolation, increased possessions and blessing in his latter life. That outcome responds to the question within the narrative without denying the despair in which it was asked.
